key_features_suggestive: new cardiac murmurs suggestive of acute mitral regurgitation or ventricular septal defect
mechanical_complications.recommended_action: Immediate echocardiographic assessment when mechanical complications are suspected.
management_notes: Temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS) may be used to improve pre‑operative clinical/haemodynamic status or prophylactically, but more data are required to confirm clinical benefit.

Surgery is currently regarded as the treatment of choice for patients with ACS and mechanical complications; percutaneous strategies occasionally used in selected high‑risk or contraindicated surgical candidates.
Multidisciplinary approach essential across all stages of care, including discussion of palliative care where appropriate.
Consider intra‑aortic balloon pump (IABP) for ACS‑related mechanical complications while awaiting surgery.

epidemiology.general_trend: Incidence has declined with reperfusion and antithrombotic therapies, but LV thrombus remains relatively common, especially after anterior STEMI.
reported_rates: >9% of patients after anterior STEMI (large meta‑analysis)
CMR-reported LV thrombi up to 6.3% of all STEMI patients
CMR-reported LV thrombi in 12.2% of anterior STEMI patients

imaging_recommendations.first_line: Echocardiography remains the first‑line imaging test for detection of LV thrombus.
adjuncts: Contrast echocardiography may be considered when the apex is not well visualized on regular echocardiography.
Cardiac MRI (CMR) is the gold standard imaging modality for diagnosis and assessment of LV thrombi and should be considered when echocardiographic images are equivocal or patient is high risk.
imaging_recommendations.clinical_observation: LV thrombi not evident on echocardiography but detected by CMR have similar clinical outcomes to those evident on echocardiography, suggesting echocardiography may underestimate incidence.

timing_of_imaging.note: Identification of LV thrombus increases in the first 2 weeks post‑MI.
timing_of_imaging.recommendation: Delayed imaging at about 2 weeks in high‑risk patients may be of value because LV thrombi can develop following hospital discharge.

anticoagulation_management.recommendation: Once LV thrombus is diagnosed, oral anticoagulant (OAC) therapy (warfarin or NOAC) should be considered for approximately 3–6 months.
anticoagulation_management.guidance: Duration should be guided by repeated echocardiography or CMR, bleeding risk assessment, and the need for concomitant antiplatelet therapy.
anticoagulation_management.evidence_gaps: Lack of prospective randomized data on optimal anticoagulation regimen, duration, and management with concomitant antiplatelet therapy.
